text:
MEMORANDUM
TO: Michael Torres, Partner
FROM: Associate
DATE: March 18, 2026
RE: Defenses to Hague Convention Petition in In re Rivera (Prospective)

I. HABITUAL RESIDENCE INQUIRY

The Supreme Court has instructed courts to consider "all circumstances relevant to the child's connection to a particular country." Monasky v. Taglieri, 140 S. Ct. 719, 726 (2020). The inquiry focuses on the child's perspective and requires a factual, holistic analysis. Id. at 727.

See Paris v. Brown, No. 24-4950, 2025 WL 6348902, at *5 (9th Cir. Oct. 3, 2025). The Ninth Circuit in Paris emphasized that "courts should not mechanically apply prior residence but must examine whether the family had a shared understanding that the move represented a permanent change." Id.

II. GRAVE RISK UNDER ARTICLE 13(b)

Walsh v. Walsh, 221 F.3d 204, 220 (1st Cir. 2000) (holding that father's "physical violence against both his wife and his children" established grave risk). Gaudin v. Remis, 415 F.3d 1028, 1036 (9th Cir. 2005).

Abouelmagd v. Semeniuk, 2025 WL 3042413, at *4 (E.D.N.Y. Oct. 31, 2025). The court rejected a grave risk defense where the mother had not produced "any real time reports" from Canadian authorities. The court further noted that "the existence of a protective order in the requested state does not, standing alone, establish that the courts of the habitual residence cannot provide adequate protection." Id.

Bassat v. Dana, No. 25-10915, 2025 WL 3987654, at *8 (11th Cir. Aug. 11, 2025). The court held that there was "testimony that described the father as engaging in other harmful actions that endangered the children's lives." The court emphasized that "serious allegations" of violence, if credited, can satisfy the grave risk standard. Id.

In Figueredo v. Rojas, 123 F.4th 1298, 1310 (11th Cir. 2025), the court held that "a child's precarious immigration status in the requested state, standing alone, does not constitute a grave risk under Article 13(b), but may be considered as part of the totality of circumstances when evaluating whether return would be intolerable."

III. THE CHILD'S OBJECTION DEFENSE

See England v. England, 234 F.3d 268, 272-73 (5th Cir. 2000); Anderson v. Acree, 250 F. Supp. 2d 876, 882 (S.D. Ohio 2002).

Nguyen v. Tran, 2025 WL 4567890, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 15, 2025). The court credited a ten-year-old's objection where the child expressed "specific fears about the father's anger and recounted particular incidents of verbal abuse." The court emphasized that "generalized preferences for remaining with the mother are insufficient; the objection must be particularized and reflect the child's independent views." Id. at *7.

The Ninth Circuit has held that courts must assess whether the child's objection is "autonomous" rather than merely reflecting the taking parent's wishes. Gaudin, 415 F.3d at 1045.

IV. ACQUIESCENCE UNDER ARTICLE 13(a)

Baxter v. Baxter, 423 F.3d 363, 371 (3d Cir. 2005).

Williams v. Sato, 2025 WL 2345678, at *8 (D. Or. June 4, 2025). The court held that "post-removal expressions of support for the child's new living arrangement, when later revoked, do not constitute acquiescence absent detrimental reliance by the taking parent."

V. THE SETTLEMENT DEFENSE

Lozano v. Montoya Alvarez, 572 U.S. 1, 17 (2014).

Rodrigues da Silva v. Silveira da Silva, 122 F.4th 356, 367 (1st Cir. 2025). The court held that "a 'now settled' child need not have a perfect or flawless life; we ask only if the constellation of facts shows a child with significant connections demonstrating a secure, stable, and permanent life in his or her new environment." The court found a child settled where he had "a loving, financially stable immediate family; has become acclimated to his school environment; has an extended step-family nearby; and is participating in various community activities." Id. at 369.

VI. THE FUGITIVE-DISENTITLEMENT DOCTRINE

In Paris v. Brown, the court held that the fugitive-disentitlement doctrine "must be narrowly applied in civil cases." Paris, 2025 WL 6348902, at *8.
